rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-2.2 - two-year (2017-2018) split-plot field experiment in a commercial Cabernet Sauvignon vineyard, Red Mountain AVA, Washington, comparing DRZ and surface drip at three irrigation rates. Q2: Section 3.5 and Table 3 - irrigation method had significant effects on yield in both years, with about 9% (2017) and 12% (2018) higher yield under DRZ than SD across rates (10.0 vs 9.2 t/ha; 10.4 vs 9.3 t/ha). Q4: Section 3.3, Fig. 3, Table 1 - midday stem water potential measured by pressure chamber was 10-14% higher under DRZ after veraison in both years, i.e. the lower plant water stress through which authors explain higher yield (Discussion: plants not under water stress have more resources for production). Q8: Discussion/Conclusions - study described as an initial step; reduced soil evaporation and deep rooting proposed as reasons but stated to need testing in future studies; a long-term (e.g. 10-year) study said to be needed to define desirable conditions; result restricted to loamy sand soil in a semi-arid climate; PVC assumed to have no effect on soil.
rows.notes: Yield measured by a single method (hand-harvest weighing); no triangulation. Soil evaporation, the primary hypothesised mechanism, was not measured; only plant water status (stem water potential) and root counts in 0-60 cm. Single site, soil, crop and climate; plot-scale within a commercial vineyard. No conditions for the effect stated from own findings (soil-texture discussion draws on literature). Table 3 gives yield means with letter groupings only; no SD/SE/CI for yield, and the 9-12% range is between years, not a dispersion measure.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-2.2 - own two-year field experiment (DRZ vs surface drip, three rates, three blocks). Q2: Section 3.5-3.6 and Table 3 - DRZ gave ~9% and 12% higher yield and 9-11% higher WUEc than SD in 2017 and 2018, with no rate x method interaction; Abstract/Discussion note the two years differed in weather yet treatment effects on yield and WUEc were unchanged. Q4: Section 3.3, Fig. 3, Table 1 - stem water potential (plant water stress) measured and found 10-14% higher under DRZ after veraison, the intermediate through which authors attribute higher yield and WUEc. Q8: Discussion/Conclusions - initial step, mechanisms (reduced evaporation, deep roots) need testing, long-term study needed, results stated for loamy sand soil in semi-arid climate.
rows.notes: The review's passage says DRZ was contrasted with 'SDI'; the study's comparator was surface drip irrigation (SD), with DRZ itself being the subsurface strategy - a comparator mislabelling by the review, but the DRZ yield/WUEc result itself is the study's own. Single measurement method for yield and WUEc; single site/soil/crop; plot-scale; no dispersion measures for yield or WUEc in Table 3 (letters and significance stars only).

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-2.2 - own two-year field experiment. Q2: Section 3.6 and Table 3 - WUEc (yield per unit of irrigation plus rainfall from bud break to harvest, Section 2.8) significantly affected by method in both years; DRZ improved WUEc by 9-11% over SD (38.3 vs 35.1 and 43.8 vs 39.3 kg/ha/mm); no interaction with rate. Q4: Section 3.3/Fig. 3 - midday stem water potential measured, 10-14% higher under DRZ after veraison, i.e. the plant-water-status link through which equal applied water produced more yield and hence higher WUEc. Q8: Discussion/Conclusions - initial step; reduced soil water evaporation as mechanism needs testing in future studies; long-term study needed; results confined to loamy sand, semi-arid climate.
rows.notes: WUEc derived from the same yield measurement and metered water applied; no independent second method. Soil evaporation (the water-saving mechanism itself) was not measured; WUEc gains arise from yield at identical water input. Single site, soil, crop, climate; plot scale; no SD/SE/CI reported for WUEc. Review passage mislabels the comparator as SDI (study compared against surface drip).

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-2.2 - own field experiment. Q2: Section 3.3, Fig. 3, Table 1 - grapevines under DRZ showed significantly 10-14% higher midday stem water potential than SD after veraison in both years, under deficit irrigation during the period of extremely limited rainfall (fruit set to harvest, Supplemental Table 1), i.e. reduced water stress; Section 3.4 shows 48-67% fewer roots in 0-60 cm under DRZ at high/moderate rates. Q8: Conclusions - deep root system and reduced evaporation as reasons for lower diurnal water stress are stated as needing testing in future studies; study described as an initial step; long-term study needed.
rows.notes: The study directly measured lower water stress (stem water potential) under DRZ, which supports the alleviation part of the passage. Deep rooting below 60 cm was inferred from fewer shallow roots, not measured, and soil water content under treatments was not reported, so the intermediate variable is not measured (Q4 no). Single method (pressure chamber) for water stress; single site/crop/soil; plot scale; Fig. 3 caption reports letter groupings (n=9) with no error bars or dispersion measures. The 'modify berry morphology by adjusting water' part relates to irrigation rate, not DRZ specifically. Review passage mislabels comparator as SDI.

notes: Full text available; Table 2 is garbled by rotated layout but values are legible. Study compares direct root-zone irrigation (a subsurface drip variant) against surface drip, not conventional buried-line SDI as some review passages state.
